definitions.text: Aaron was a Levite, son of Amram and Jochebed, and brother of Moses and Miriam. He married Elisheba and had four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. God appointed him as spokesman, or "prophet," for Moses before Pharaoh, and the two together led Israel out of Egypt and through the wilderness, conveying God's commands and numbering the people. Aaron and his sons were clothed and consecrated as priests serving at the tabernacle altar, with the priestly garments and offerings passing to his descendants. He made the golden calf while the people demanded gods, and Moses rebuked him. His rod was kept before the testimony as a sign against rebels. He died at 123 on Mount Hor; his descendants, "the house of Aaron," formed the priesthood.
definitions.notes: The birth and death dates in the graph (1574–1452 BC) are editorial and not stated in the verses; Numbers 33:39 gives only his age of 123 at death.

definitions.text: Abana is a river of Damascus, named only once in the Bible. When Naaman the Syrian was told to wash in the Jordan, he protested that Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, were better than all the waters of Israel, and he went away angry (2Kgs.5.12). The Hebrew margin gives the alternative reading "Amanah." It is commonly identified with the modern Barada River, which flows past Damascus.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions Abana, and it gives no description of the river beyond its association with Damascus. The spelling "Amanah" appears as a marginal variant. The identification with the Barada is a later geographical judgement rather than a biblical statement.

definitions.text: Abiel was a Benjamite, son of Zeror, named in the ancestry of King Saul. 1 Samuel 9:1 calls Kish, Saul's father, "the son of Abiel," while 1 Samuel 14:51 says that Ner, the father of Abner, was the son of Abiel; the Chronicles genealogies instead have Ner fathering Kish, who fathered Saul. The graph also equates Abiel with Ner and with Jehiel, called the father (founder) of Gibeon, whose wife was Maachah, making him the ancestor of a large family including Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher and Mikloth. The name is shared by more than one person in the Bible.
definitions.notes: The sources conflict on whether Kish was Abiel's son (1 Sam 9:1) or grandson through Ner (1 Sam 14:51; 1 Chr 8:33; 9:39). The identification of Abiel with Ner and with Jehiel of Gibeon comes from the graph's relationships, not from any verse supplied; the list of children derives from the Jehiel genealogy (1 Chr 9:36-37), which is not among the citable verses.

definitions.text: Ashur is a man in the genealogies of Judah, born to Hezron by his wife Abiah after Hezron's death in Calebephratah. He is called "the father of Tekoa," a phrase the genealogies use for the founder or ancestor of that town. He had two wives, Helah and Naarah, through whom the record lists children including Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni, Haahashtari, Zereth, Jezoar, Ethnan and Coz. Through Hezron he is linked with Caleb, Jerahmeel and Ram.
definitions.notes: Only two verses mention him, both purely genealogical; nothing is recorded of his life. The division of his children between Helah and Naarah comes from the verses following 1Chr.4.5, which were not supplied.

definitions.text: Atad is the site of a threshing floor "beyond Jordan" where Joseph and his company stopped while carrying Jacob's body for burial, holding seven days of loud mourning. When the Canaanites living in the area saw the mourning, they remarked on how grievous it was for the Egyptians, and the place was renamed Abel-mizraim. Its exact location is unknown.
definitions.notes: Only two verses mention Atad, and no coordinates are recorded. The phrase "beyond Jordan" is ambiguous as to which side of the river is meant; Easton's guess that it lay near Hebron is not supported by the text. Easton also links the name to a thorn or buckthorn plant, which is an etymological suggestion rather than a stated fact.

definitions.text: Baal-zephon was a place in Egypt used as a landmark for one of Israel's camping sites during the exodus. Israel was told to turn back and camp before Pihahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon, and they pitched there by the sea. Numbers lists the same stage: after leaving Etham they turned to Pihahiroth, which lies before Baal-zephon, and camped before Migdol. It was there that Pharaoh's horses, chariots, horsemen and army overtook the Israelites. The texts place it near a body of water, traditionally identified with a site on the Gulf of Suez, but its exact location is not certain.
definitions.notes: Baal-zephon appears only as a reference point in three verses; nothing is said about the place itself. The proposed coordinates and the identification with a site on the Gulf of Suez (Easton suggests Jebel Deraj or Kulalah) are conjectural, as is the related route of the exodus.

definitions.text: The Birth of Simeon is the account in Genesis 29:33 of Leah bearing a second son to Jacob. Leah said that the LORD had heard she was hated and had therefore given her this son as well, and she named him Simeon. The graph dates the event to about 1757 BC and lists Jacob (Israel), Leah and Simeon as those involved.
definitions.notes: Only one verse is supplied; the date of about 1757 BC comes from the graph's chronology, not from the text.

definitions.text: Cherith is a brook or seasonal stream valley named in the Bible only in connection with Elijah. Told to go eastward and hide himself, Elijah went and lived beside the brook Cherith, which the text locates "before Jordan" — that is, facing or opening toward the Jordan River. Nothing else is recorded about the site, and its exact position is uncertain; the traditional identifications place it in a ravine on one or other side of the Jordan near Jericho or in Gilead.
definitions.notes: Only two verses mention Cherith, and neither fixes its location beyond "before Jordan." Whether it lay east or west of the Jordan is disputed; the coordinates given in the graph are marked rough.

definitions.text: The Creation of all things is the opening narrative of Genesis, in which God makes the heavens and the earth over a sequence of seven days. The earth begins formless, dark and covered with water, with the Spirit of God moving over it (Gen.1.1-Gen.1.2). God then speaks light into being and separates light from darkness (Gen.1.3-Gen.1.5), makes the firmament (Gen.1.6-Gen.1.8), gathers the seas and brings forth plants (Gen.1.9-Gen.1.13), sets the sun, moon and stars (Gen.1.14-Gen.1.19), fills sea and sky with living creatures (Gen.1.20-Gen.1.23), and makes land animals and humankind, male and female, in his own image, giving them dominion (Gen.1.24-Gen.1.28). Pronouncing it all very good, God rests on the seventh day and blesses it (Gen.1.31-Gen.2.3).
definitions.notes: The date of 4004 BC comes from a traditional chronology, not from the text itself. The passage names God and the Spirit of God (Gen.1.2); the listing of Jesus Christ among the participants is not stated in these verses, though Gen.1.26 uses plural language ("Let us make man").

definitions.text: Delilah was a woman of the valley of Sorek whom Samson loved. She repeatedly pressed him to reveal the source of his great strength and how he might be bound, accusing him of mocking her and telling her lies when his answers failed. She bound him with new ropes while men lay in wait in an inner room, but he broke them like thread. She also tried weaving the seven locks of his hair into a web. When he finally told her all his heart, she summoned the lords of the Philistines, who came to her bringing money.
definitions.notes: The verses supplied do not state her nationality or family; Easton's calls her a Philistine woman, but the text here only places her in the valley of Sorek.

definitions.text: The Deliverance by Ehud is the episode in Judges 3 in which Israel, after crying to the LORD during Moab's rule, was freed by Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite. Sent with tribute to Eglon king of Moab, Ehud carried a hidden two-edged dagger strapped to his right thigh. After delivering the tribute and dismissing his companions, he returned, claimed a secret message, and killed the king alone in his upper chamber, then locked the doors and escaped while servants delayed. Sounding a trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim, he led Israel to seize the Jordan fords and kill about ten thousand Moabites. Moab was subdued, and the land had rest for eighty years.
definitions.notes: The graph's date (1360 BC) and 62-year duration are editorial reckonings; the text itself says the land rested eighty years (Judg.3.30).

definitions.text: Fair Havens was a harbour or anchorage on the island of Crete, reached with difficulty by the ship carrying Paul on his voyage to Rome. Acts notes that the city of Lasea lay nearby. The name appears only once in the Bible, in the account of that journey, where the vessel put in along the Cretan coast after struggling against the wind.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions Fair Havens, and it gives no detail beyond its proximity to Lasea. Easton's additional account of the ship wintering there and the later shipwreck comes from surrounding verses not supplied here; the precise site is identified only by modern coordinates, not by the text.

definitions.text: Haggith was one of David's wives and the mother of Adonijah, listed as David's fourth son among those born at Hebron (2 Samuel 3:4; 1 Chronicles 3:2). She herself never speaks or acts in the narrative; she appears only in the repeated phrase "Adonijah the son of Haggith," used when Adonijah claimed the throne for himself, when Nathan reported this to Bathsheba, and when Adonijah later approached Bathsheba (1 Kings 1:5, 11; 2:13).
definitions.notes: Nothing is recorded of Haggith's family, origin or actions; Easton's gloss on her name and the note about Adonijah's beauty are not supported by the supplied verses.

definitions.text: Hezron is a place named only once, as a point on the southern boundary line of the tribe of Judah. The border ran south to Maaleh-acrabbim, passed on to Zin, went up south of Kadesh-barnea, passed along to Hezron, then up to Adar and around to Karkaa (Josh.15.3). Nothing else is recorded about it, and its exact site is unknown.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions this place, and it gives no description beyond its position in a boundary list. The coordinates recorded in the graph fall in the far north and conflict with the verse's southern setting; the identification is uncertain. The name Hezron is also borne by several persons elsewhere in the Bible.

definitions.text: Jahath was a man of the tribe of Judah, son of Reaiah and grandson of Shobal. He was the father of Ahumai and Lahad, whose descendants are called the families of the Zorathites. He appears only in this genealogical note.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions this Jahath, and it gives nothing beyond his place in a genealogy. The name is borne by several other men in the Bible (chiefly Levites), so references to "Jahath" elsewhere should not be assumed to be this person.

definitions.text: Jesus in Capernaum refers to Jesus leaving Nazareth and settling in Capernaum, a city of Galilee on the lake shore in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matt.4.13; Luke.4.31). Matthew presents the move as fulfilling words of the prophet Isaiah about the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, "Galilee of the Gentiles," where people sitting in darkness saw a great light (Matt.4.14-16). From this point Jesus began to preach, "Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matt.4.17), and Luke notes that he taught in Capernaum on the sabbath days (Luke.4.31). The graph places the move after his rejection at Nazareth, around AD 27.
definitions.notes: The date (AD 27) and the one-day duration are editorial assignments of the graph, not stated in the verses; Luke's "sabbath days" implies a longer stay than a single day.

definitions.text: Joseph, son of Juda (Judah), is a man named only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. He appears there as the father of Semei and the son of Juda, within the line descending through Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him; the genealogy supplies only his place in the sequence of names. Other men named Joseph also occur in the same list, so the name alone does not distinguish him.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions him, and it gives no details beyond his father and son. Because Joseph is a common name in Luke's genealogy, identification of this particular Joseph rests entirely on his position in the list.

definitions.text: Lahmam was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah, named only once in the Bible. It appears in Joshua's list of Judah's settlements between Cabbon and Kithlish, in a group of towns belonging to the low-lying western district. Nothing else is recorded about it; the site is placed by modern geographers in the region southwest of Jerusalem, but the identification is not certain.
definitions.notes: Only a single verse mentions Lahmam, and it supplies nothing beyond the name and its position in a list. The coordinates given in the graph reflect a proposed modern identification, not information stated in the text.

definitions.text: The Lifetime of Arphaxad is the span of years recorded for Arphaxad in the genealogy of Genesis 11. He was 35 years old when he fathered Salah, and he lived 403 years afterward, during which he had further sons and daughters — a total of 438 years. The graph dates the start of this period, his birth, to about 2346 BC, following a traditional chronology. The two verses give no other details about his life.
definitions.notes: The total of 438 years is a sum of the two figures given; the text itself does not state it. The 2346 BC date comes from a calculated chronology, not from the verses.

definitions.text: Michael was a Levite named in a genealogy in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Baaseiah and the father of Shimea, appearing in a list of ancestors traced back through the tribe of Levi. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several different men named Michael appear in the Bible, so this one is identified only by his place in this family line.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions him, and it gives no information beyond his father and son. Easton's calls him a Gershonite Levite, but the supplied verse itself does not state the Levite clan.

definitions.text: The Mission to Iconium was a stage of Paul and Barnabas's first missionary journey, following their work at Antioch in Pisidia. In Iconium the two went together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a large number of both Jews and Greeks believed (Acts 14:1). Jews who did not believe turned the Gentiles against the visiting preachers, but Paul and Barnabas stayed a long time, speaking boldly, and signs and wonders were done by their hands (Acts 14:2-3). The city split into factions, some siding with the Jews and some with the apostles, until Gentiles, Jews and their rulers joined in an attempt to mistreat and stone them (Acts 14:4-5).
definitions.notes: The date (AD 46) and the five-month duration are from the graph, not the text; Acts says only that they stayed "long time." The cited passage breaks off mid-sentence at Acts 14:5, so the outcome of the assault is not included.

definitions.text: Mount Shapher (spelled Mount Shepher in modern versions) was one of the camping places of the Israelites during their journey through the wilderness. According to the list of stages in Numbers 33, they came to it from Kehelathah and left it to camp at Haradah. The mountain is named only in these two verses, and nothing else is recorded about it; its exact location is uncertain, though it is placed roughly in the region south of the Dead Sea.
definitions.notes: The site is known only from the itinerary list in Numbers 33; the coordinates given in the graph are explicitly approximate and the identification of the mountain is not certain.

definitions.text: Peter's Confession "Upon this Rock" is the exchange near Caesarea Philippi in which Jesus asked his disciples who people said he was. They reported answers such as John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets. When he asked what they themselves said, Simon Peter answered, "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Mark and Luke give shorter forms). In Matthew's account Jesus called him blessed, said the Father had revealed it to him, declared "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church," promised him the keys of the kingdom of heaven with authority to bind and loose, and then charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ.
definitions.notes: The three accounts differ in detail: Luke places the question while Jesus was praying alone with the disciples rather than naming the Caesarea Philippi road, and only Matthew records the "rock," church and keys sayings. The AD 29 date and one-day duration come from the graph, not the verses.

definitions.text: Reaiah was the ancestor of a family listed among those who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. The "children of Reaiah" appear in the register of temple servants in Ezra 2:47, between the families of Gahar and Rezin, and the same group is listed again in the parallel register of Nehemiah 7:50. Nothing further is recorded about him personally. The name is shared by more than one person in the Bible, so this Reaiah should not be confused with others bearing the name.
definitions.notes: Both verses are parallel registers rather than independent accounts, and neither says anything about Reaiah himself beyond his name heading a family group. The name is shared by several biblical figures, so identification is uncertain.

definitions.text: Rehoboth is a city known in the Bible as "Rehoboth by the river," the home of Shaul (also spelled Saul), who became king of Edom after the death of Samlah (Gen.36.37; 1Chr.1.48). The two passages are parallel king lists and are the only references to this Rehoboth. The name Rehoboth is shared by more than one biblical place, and the exact site and the identity of the river are not specified in the text.
definitions.notes: Only two parallel verses mention this place, and neither names the river or locates the city. Easton's identifies it as a city on the Euphrates, but the text does not say so; the recorded coordinates point to a site in the Edom region instead, so the location is disputed. Other biblical places also bear the name Rehoboth.

definitions.text: The Reign of Hezekiah was the rule of Hezekiah son of Ahaz over Judah from Jerusalem, beginning in the third year of Hoshea king of Israel and traditionally dated from about 726 BC for 29 years. The record says he did what was right before the LORD, kept to him, and defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza. During his reign Assyria deported Israel, and in his fourteenth year Sennacherib took Judah's fortified cities; Hezekiah paid tribute from the temple and palace treasuries, and his officials Eliakim, Shebna and Joah heard Rabshakeh's challenge. Hezekiah prayed and consulted the prophet Isaiah, and Sennacherib withdrew to Nineveh. Isaiah also attended his illness and recovery, and envoys came from Babylon. He died and Manasseh his son succeeded him.
definitions.notes: The 726 BC date and 29-year length come from the graph's chronology, not from the sampled verses; biblical dating is given relative to Hoshea's reign.

definitions.text: The Reign of Jehoshaphat was the 25-year rule of Jehoshaphat son of Asa over Judah from Jerusalem, begun in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel when Jehoshaphat was thirty-five; his mother was Azubah daughter of Shilhi (1Kgs.22.41-42). He followed the ways of his father Asa and did what was right in the LORD's eyes, though the high places remained in use for sacrifice and incense (1Kgs.22.43). He made peace with the king of Israel (1Kgs.22.44) and removed those remaining from Asa's time described as sodomites (1Kgs.22.46). Edom had no king, only a deputy (1Kgs.22.47). His ships built for gold at Ophir were wrecked at Ezion-geber, and he refused Ahaziah's offer of joint crews (1Kgs.22.48-49). He was buried in the city of David and succeeded by his son Jehoram (1Kgs.22.50).
definitions.notes:
The date of 914 BC is an editorial estimate, not stated in the verses; the passage dates the accession only relative to Ahab's fourth year.

definitions.text: Simeon was a man living in Jerusalem, described as just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, with the Holy Spirit upon him (Luke 2:25). When Mary and the child Jesus came to the temple, Simeon blessed them and told Mary that the child was appointed for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and as a sign that would be spoken against (Luke 2:34). The name Simeon is shared by several different people in the Bible.
definitions.notes: Only two verses are supplied, so nothing is known here beyond Simeon's piety and his words in the temple; the name belongs to several distinct biblical figures and should not be confused with them.

definitions.text: Tabor is a mountain in northern Israel, in the hill country west of the Sea of Galilee. It marked the boundary of a tribal territory described in Joshua, where the border reached Tabor, Shahazimah and Bethshemesh before ending at the Jordan. Gideon questioned the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna about the men they had killed at Tabor, who resembled royal sons. The Psalms pair Tabor with Hermon as mountains that rejoice in the LORD's name, and Jeremiah uses Tabor's standing "among the mountains," like Carmel by the sea, as an image of certainty. Hosea rebukes leaders for being "a net spread upon Tabor."
definitions.notes: The supplied verses do not state Tabor's exact height, tribal owner, or any battle fought on it; Easton's identification with Jebel et-Tur and its link to Barak and to the transfiguration is outside the cited verses, and Easton himself calls the transfiguration tradition disputed.

definitions.text: An episode in Jericho, dated in the graph to about AD 30, as Jesus travelled toward Jerusalem. Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector who was short, climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus passing; Jesus told him to come down and said he would stay at his house, which drew complaints that he was lodging with a sinner. Zacchaeus promised half his goods to the poor and fourfold restitution for anything wrongly taken, and Jesus declared that salvation had come to the house. Because the crowd expected the kingdom of God to appear at once, Jesus then told the parable of a nobleman who gave ten servants a pound each to trade with until his return. He then went up to Jerusalem.
definitions.notes: The AD 30 date and one-day duration come from the graph, not the text.
